strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck in autoregressive structured prediction: decoder latency. On ASE, Fast SceneScript-SSD with 10 heads reduces decoding latency from 382 ms to 75 ms (5.09x) while retaining nearly the same mean test F1 (0.912 versus 0.915). On Structured3D, it reduces latency from 1176 ms to 211 ms while improving mean F1 from 0.774 to 0.790.

The method combines multi-token prediction with two sensible reliability mechanisms. The adaptation of self-speculative decoding to tolerate small discrepancies in numerical tokens is well motivated for quantized geometric outputs, while confidence-guided decoding avoids a separate verification pass.

The parameter-sharing design materially improves efficiency: the 10-head SSD model has 15.05M decoder parameters, compared with 26.43M for the straightforward MTP baseline. The ablation comparing shared and unshared variants supports the claim that sharing does not reduce accuracy.

The evaluation covers two substantially different indoor-scene datasets, reports validation and held-out test performance, compares against the released SceneScript model and a specialized floorplan method, and includes component, tolerance, decoding-strategy, and parameter-sharing ablations.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, and the tables expose the principal accuracy-latency-parameter tradeoffs. Qualitative examples are consistent with the quantitative finding that unfiltered MTP often produces incomplete layouts.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrower than the framing. Despite claims about language-based perception models and preserved generality, experiments cover only 3D layout estimation and only the SceneScript architecture. No object detection, part reconstruction, 2D structured prediction, or alternative structured-language model is tested, so transfer beyond this specific setting remains speculative.

Efficiency reporting is limited to language-decoder latency and decoder parameter count. End-to-end latency, 3D-encoder cost, peak memory, FLOPs, sequence-length dependence, and throughput at different batch sizes are absent. The comparison with RoomFormer is especially difficult to interpret because the reported parameter metric excludes the encoders and therefore is not a full-model comparison.

Latency reproducibility is insufficient. The paper names an RTX 2080 Ti but omits batch size, precision, software stack, warm-up and synchronization procedure, number of timed runs, variability, and whether all filtering and sequence-processing overhead is included. No uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are reported for either latency or F1.

Several details needed to reproduce CGD are missing, most notably its inference confidence threshold epsilon and how that threshold is selected. The exact recurrence, residual structure, and positional information in the shared projection blocks are also underspecified, as are decoding and termination settings.

The novelty is useful but largely compositional: MTP, speculative verification, confidence-based filtering, and head sharing are established ideas. The numerical-token tolerance and learned agreement confidence are task-aware adaptations, but the paper does not provide a deeper analysis showing when they generalize or fail.

SSD's tolerance-based verification is no longer lossless speculative decoding: it may retain a draft numerical token that differs from the primary-head prediction, which can alter later autoregressive context. The paper demonstrates good aggregate F1 but does not analyze accumulated geometric error, malformed-program rates, validity constraints, or worst-case failures.

The evidence for hyperparameter robustness is limited. Tau is ablated only on ASE validation, competing confidence thresholds are manually selected to maximize speed without accuracy loss, and the claimed degradation beyond 10 heads is deferred to unprovided supplementary material. These choices make the operating-point comparisons less conclusive.

Overall, the supported accuracy-speed improvement is strong enough for a weak accept, but the score is moderated by limited task generalization, incomplete end-to-end efficiency accounting, and missing reproducibility details.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of autoregressive structured prediction. Reported decoder latency improves substantially over SceneScript: 5.09× on ASE and 5.57× on Structured3D, while mean F1 remains close to or above the baseline.
The evaluation includes two datasets, SSD and confidence-guided decoding variants, several MTP head counts, parameter counts, latency, token acceptance, per-class F1, and qualitative examples.

The head-sharing mechanism is empirically useful: at eight heads, SSD reduces decoder parameters from 23.67M for conventional MTP to 15.05M while recovering most of the accuracy lost by unfiltered MTP.
The paper is generally easy to follow and clearly illustrates the motivation, architecture, and speed–accuracy–parameter trade-off.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The main framework combines established multi-token prediction and self-speculative decoding with SceneScript. The proposed CGD predicts agreement with the first head rather than correctness against ground truth; it can therefore assign high confidence to consistently wrong predictions. No calibration, error-detection, or failure-case analysis establishes that this score reliably measures correctness.

Efficiency accounting is insufficiently clear. SSD requires an additional verification forward pass, yet alpha is described as accepted tokens per decoder inference and reported near nine for ten heads. The manuscript does not explain whether verification passes are included in this denominator or reused for drafting. Consequently, claims such as predicting nine tokens per decoder step are not adequately supported, even though the wall-clock latency results remain informative.

The latency study omits important protocol details, including precision, batch size, sequence-length statistics, warm-up and repetition counts, variance, KV-cache use, and whether encoder time is included. No memory or end-to-end throughput results are given. Moreover, the specialized RoomFormer baseline remains much faster on Structured3D (54 ms versus 211–269 ms).

The evidence does not substantiate the claimed generality. Experiments cover only layout estimation and three structural classes on ASE and Structured3D; object detection, part reconstruction, real-scan robustness, and other claimed applications are not evaluated. Thus, preservation of SceneScript's broader versatility is assumed rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is materially limited: the critical CGD threshold epsilon is not reported; the shared projection block's positional or recurrent mapping is not defined mathematically; inference sampling is unspecified; and learning-rate milestones and detailed timing procedures are absent. The manuscript also refers to supplementary experiments that are not present in the supplied paper.

Accuracy differences lack uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. On ASE, Fast SceneScript is slightly below the trained SceneScript baseline (0.910–0.913 versus 0.915 mean F1), while several claimed improvements elsewhere are small. Without variance, it is unclear which differences are meaningful.

Some headline parameter claims are selective: the approximately 7.5% decoder overhead applies to SSD (15.05M versus 14.00M), whereas CGD uses 16.10M, roughly 15% overhead. Counts also exclude the 3D encoder, limiting conclusions about whole-system parameter efficiency. Overall, the useful engineering results do not overcome the modest originality and insufficiently specified evidence for the central reliability and efficiency claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in autoregressive 3D scene-layout generation and presents a coherent combination of multi-token prediction, reliability filtering, and parameter sharing.

The efficiency gains are substantial under matched SceneScript comparisons: on ASE, SSD with 10 heads reduces latency from 382 ms to 75 ms (5.09×) while retaining nearly the same mean test F1 (0.912 versus 0.915); on Structured3D, it reduces latency from 1176 ms to 211 ms while improving mean F1 from 0.774 to 0.790.

The evaluation covers two datasets, both validation and held-out test results where applicable, accuracy/latency/parameter trade-offs, qualitative examples, and useful ablations of numerical tolerance, confidence scoring, and head sharing.

The parameter-efficient design is practically valuable: SSD adds only about 7.5% decoder parameters over SceneScript, while the ablation indicates that sharing reduces parameters substantially without hurting accuracy.

The manuscript is clear and well organized, and its central empirical conclusion—that structured outputs permit many reliable tokens to be accepted per decoding step—is directly supported by the reported acceptance rates.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is incremental: multi-token heads, self-speculative verification, confidence-based filtering, and parameter sharing build closely on existing decoding ideas. The main contribution is their adaptation and effective integration for structured 3D outputs rather than a fundamentally new decoding principle.

The evidence supports layout estimation only. Claims that the framework preserves the versatility of perception-generalist models or can extend to object detection and part reconstruction remain untested; both benchmarks also represent closely related indoor-layout settings.

The assertion that accuracy is preserved is not statistically established. ASE mean test F1 decreases from 0.915 to 0.912–0.913, and no repeated runs, error bars, or significance analysis are reported. This is a small limitation rather than a contradiction of the overall trade-off.

Efficiency evaluation is confined to one RTX 2080 Ti and reports latency without latency variance, memory consumption, batch-size sensitivity, sequence-length breakdowns, or a precise accounting of whether all encoder and verification costs are included. This limits how confidently the speedups transfer to other deployment regimes.

Important reproducibility details are missing from the manuscript, notably the CGD inference threshold ε, exact projection-block dimensions/application across future positions, decoding settings, and sufficient implementation detail for reconstructing the confidence targets and verification pipeline. Reliance on unspecified supplementary material does not resolve these omissions in the provided submission.

The comparison with RoomFormer mixes a task-specialized architecture with a language-based model and counts only decoder parameters, so it does not establish overall model-size or end-to-end efficiency superiority. The primary matched SceneScript comparisons are substantially more convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear practical bottleneck in language-based 3D perception: autoregressive decoding latency. The reported decoder speedups are substantial and consistent across layout estimation and object detection, including 5.09× on ASE layout, 5.57× on Structured3D layout, and 5.14× on ASE detection.

The accuracy-efficiency trade-off is convincing. Token filtering largely recovers the severe degradation of naive MTP: on ASE layout with 10 heads, mean test F1 improves from 0.814 for naive MTP to 0.912 for SSD, close to the 0.915 SceneScript baseline, while retaining a large latency reduction.

Evaluation covers two tasks and three datasets, including synthetic ASE and Structured3D as well as real-world SceneCAD. The consistent improvements over the accelerated baseline support usefulness beyond one benchmark.

The experiments separate SSD and CGD, study numerical-token tolerance, compare CGD against softmax- and product-threshold filtering, vary the number of heads and thresholds, and evaluate parameter sharing. These ablations provide reasonable support for the main design choices.

The shared-head projection mechanism provides meaningful parameter savings: the SSD model uses 15.05M decoder parameters versus 23.67M for conventional eight-head MTP, while maintaining substantially better accuracy. The method and figures are generally clear, and failure cases are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. MTP, self-speculative decoding, learned confidence prediction, and head sharing are established ideas; the main contribution is their adaptation and engineering for SceneScript-style structured 3D outputs. The paper does not deeply establish which properties of structured visual languages require fundamentally new methodology.

The headline speedups concern decoding alone, excluding the 3D encoder and other end-to-end processing. Results are reported on only an RTX 2080 Ti, without peak memory, throughput, sequence-length stratification, repeated timing variation, or full-pipeline latency. Consequently, the practical system-level speedup is not established.

Several accuracy-preservation claims are slightly overstated. On ASE layout, Fast SceneScript reaches 0.910–0.913 test F1 versus 0.915 for the matched 60-epoch baseline and 0.920 for the 90-epoch baseline in the supplement. No multi-seed results or confidence intervals are provided, so small gains and losses cannot be distinguished from training variance.

Baseline training is not completely controlled: MTP models are initialized from an already trained NTP model and receive additional training, whereas the principal NTP comparison uses the shorter 60-epoch schedule. The longer-trained NTP result improves to 0.920, but it is not used in the main tables. This does not undermine the latency result, but weakens claims about matched accuracy or beneficial regularization.

CGD is trained to predict agreement with the first head rather than correctness. This can accept mutually consistent but incorrect predictions, and the evidence is limited to aggregate downstream F1. Calibration, precision/recall of the confidence decision, error propagation, and behavior under distribution shift are not analyzed.

The evaluation breadth for object detection is limited: ASE annotations are pseudo-labels produced by TR3D from dense ground-truth depth, SceneCAD is small, and no specialized or additional language-based detector is included. Thus, broad claims about 3D scene understanding are stronger than the demonstrated scope.

Important reproducibility details remain incomplete, including tokenization and numerical quantization, point-cloud preprocessing, learning-rate milestones, threshold selection on non-ASE datasets, exact SSD scheduling/cache behavior, and whether every verification computation is included in the reported accepted-tokens-per-inference statistic. Code or a release commitment is also not stated.

strengths: The manuscript presents a practically useful acceleration of SceneScript, with substantial measured decoder-latency reductions: 5.09× for ASE layout estimation, 5.57× on Structured3D, and 5.14× for ASE object detection, while largely retaining the NTP baseline's F1 scores. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/211f8f3373264d4bbf71d204b77c003d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation covers two synthetic datasets and the real-world SceneCAD dataset, two perception tasks, multiple prediction-head counts, and both accuracy and efficiency metrics.

The ablations meaningfully separate numerical-token tolerance, SSD, CGD, confidence thresholds, and parameter sharing. They support the conclusion that filtering recovers much of the accuracy lost by naive MTP.
The shared-head design substantially reduces decoder parameters relative to conventional independent MTP heads; for example, the eight-head SSD model uses 15.05M parameters instead of 23.67M.
The method and supplementary material are generally clear, and failure cases involving incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan layouts are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited. MTP, self-speculative verification, confidence-based filtering, and shared prediction heads are established ideas; the principal changes are their application to SceneScript, a numerical-token tolerance rule, and an agreement-prediction head. The paper does not establish a deeper technical insight beyond this combination.

The headline efficiency evidence is incomplete. Reported latency covers decoding rather than end-to-end processing, and parameter counts cover only the language decoder. Encoder time, total parameters, peak memory, FLOPs, batch size, numerical precision, warm-up, and timing variance are absent. Consequently, the reported 5× gains do not establish an equivalent end-to-end system speedup.

The comparison with RoomFormer is not clearly commensurate: Fast SceneScript's decoder-only parameters and decoding latency appear alongside a specialized model with a different architecture and inference pipeline. This weakens claims of broader computational superiority, although comparisons against SceneScript remain useful.

Accuracy differences are reported from single runs without uncertainty. Several conclusions depend on changes of only 0.001–0.005 F1, including the claim of preserving or improving accuracy, so the evidence does not distinguish genuine improvements from training variability.

The ASE object-detection experiment relies on non-public pseudo-labels generated by TR3D from ground-truth depth. The detector checkpoint, pseudo-label generation settings, and resulting annotations are not supplied in the manuscript, materially limiting reproducibility and making this a less convincing benchmark than evaluation on public ground-truth detection labels.

CGD is trained to predict agreement with the first head rather than correctness against ground truth. Correlated errors can therefore receive high confidence. The paper provides no calibration, accepted-token error rate, or selective-risk analysis demonstrating that CGD confidence reliably tracks correctness; the softmax histograms do not answer this question.

The claimed generality remains only partially demonstrated. Experiments cover layout estimation and five-category object detection on a small set of indoor datasets, while object-part reconstruction is merely identified as a potential application. Comparisons against other language-based 3D systems such as SpatialLM are also absent.

Important reproducibility details remain underspecified, including the exact sampling/decoding policy, complete timing protocol, preprocessing, and availability of code and newly created data splits. The random ASE split further complicates comparison with future work unless the listed split files are released.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear practical limitation of language-based 3D perception: autoregressive decoding latency. Applying multi-token prediction to structured scene languages is a useful and reasonably original contribution, even though its components build on established multi-token and speculative-decoding ideas.

The empirical speed–accuracy trade-off is compelling. Relative to the retrained SceneScript baseline, Fast SceneScript preserves nearly the same ASE layout F1 (0.913 versus 0.915) while reducing decoder latency from 382 ms to 75–92 ms. Similar gains appear on Structured3D, SceneCAD, and ASE object detection, with approximately 2.6–5.6× lower reported decoding latency.

The evaluation covers two tasks, three datasets, and both synthetic and real-world data. Structured3D results are particularly encouraging: the proposed variants improve mean layout F1 from 0.774 to 0.790–0.795 while substantially reducing latency.

The ablations are informative and support the main design choices. They examine the numerical consistency tolerance, confidence thresholds, number of prediction heads, conventional softmax/product confidence baselines, supervision choices, and parameter sharing.

The shared-head design meaningfully limits parameter growth: the SSD model uses 15.05M decoder parameters compared with 14.00M for SceneScript and 23.67M for conventional eight-head MTP. Qualitative results and disclosed failure cases complement the quantitative evidence.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful implementation details in the supplement, including optimization settings, training schedules, loss weights, and network diagrams.
weaknesses: The principal efficiency metric is decoder-only latency. End-to-end latency including the 3D encoder and post-processing, peak memory, throughput, batch size, timing repetitions, warm-up procedure, and variance are not reported. Consequently, the demonstrated decoder acceleration is convincing, but the practical whole-system speedup remains uncertain.

All acceleration experiments use one relatively small SceneScript decoder. Results on another structured-language architecture, especially a larger model such as SpatialLM, would better establish that the method is a general contribution rather than a SceneScript-specific engineering improvement. The paper also mentions object-part reconstruction as a potential application but does not evaluate it.

The ASE object-detection annotations are pseudo-labels produced by TR3D from dense ground-truth depth because public ground truth is unavailable. Performance on that benchmark therefore partly measures agreement with a teacher rather than accuracy against human ground truth, and the pseudo-label generation protocol is insufficiently specified for exact reproduction. The SceneCAD results mitigate, but do not eliminate, this concern.

CGD is trained to predict agreement with the first head rather than correctness against ground truth. Agreement can be high when both predictions are wrong, so describing this output simply as token reliability is somewhat stronger than what is technically supervised. Task-level results show that the heuristic works, but calibration or error-detection metrics would be needed to substantiate reliability claims directly.

Reported differences are based on single point estimates without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or timing variability. This matters particularly for small accuracy differences such as 0.915 versus 0.913 on ASE and for the approximately 1–4 ms latency differences among some ablations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not state that code, trained models, generated detection annotations, or the referenced ASE split files will be released. Several training and timing details needed for exact replication are also absent.

Presentation refinement: the paper sometimes uses broad terms such as “inference speedup” where “decoder-only latency reduction” would be more precise, and claims of a general framework should be distinguished more carefully from the evidence obtained using a single backbone. These wording issues do not undermine the core contribution.
